title: The General and the Gardener
subtitle: Jasmine After Rain · Chapter 35 of 40
content:
The basil looked dreadful.

Iroh stood over the pot as though it had violated the terms of a peace treaty.

"It has refused every reasonable offer," he said.

"It needs water."

"That is one interpretation."

I crouched beside the pot and touched the soil. Dry as dust. The leaves at the bottom had curled in on themselves, and a thin crack ran along the earth beside the stem.

The courtyard behind the Jasmine Dragon wasn't grand. It held a row of herbs for the kitchen, a stubborn vine I had once labeled NOT TEA, and a few flowers planted because bees visited them. It smelled of warm brick and soil; a place where people could be ordinary even after doing extraordinary things.

Iroh brought a watering can and raised it.

"Not all at once," I said.

He looked at me.

"Too much water runs past the roots. Give it time."

He poured a little. We waited for it to soak in.

Lian, the neighbor on the other side of the wall, leaned over with a basket in her arms.

"Your mint is blocking my delivery path again."

Iroh looked at the stems.

"An ambitious plant."

"It's a nuisance," she answered, though she was smiling. "Can you trim it today?"

"We will," I said.

After she left, Iroh reached for the shears.

"Shall we launch the campaign?"

I looked at him.

"Let's measure how much of the path needs clearing first."

He paused.

"Very well. A campaign with boundaries."

We measured the path. The stems had grown farther than I'd realized, and removing them without checking might have left the roots exposed to the afternoon sun. We cut only the overhang and carried the trimmings to the kitchen to dry.

Mina accepted the mint with a suspicious look.

"Did you wash it?"

"Not yet," I admitted.

"Then it isn't ready for tea."

Iroh bowed.

"Our victory has been postponed."

She rolled her eyes and handed us a clean bowl.

When we returned to the courtyard, I found him staring at the empty section of path.

"You're thinking about something else," I said.

"Am I?"

"Possibly about how the garden has failed to acknowledge your leadership."

He laughed, but the sound faded.

"I used to think every problem could be arranged into a battle. Even when I wanted to grow something."

"Do you still?"

"Sometimes. There were years when I was praised for conquering things. I still reach for those words before I find better ones."

I sat beside him.

"Do the plants mind?"

"No. But I do."

He looked toward the empty chair under the tree.

"Lu Ten liked gardens," he said. "He liked the way they kept changing after the work was done. He would put his chair somewhere new every day to see what he had missed."

I didn't answer immediately. The memory belonged to him; I did not want to make it into a lesson about how much happier he ought to be now.

"Would you like the chair moved?" I asked.

"Perhaps tomorrow."

"Then tomorrow."

Iroh took the trowel and turned it over in his hands.

"Will you show me how to repot the basil? Without pretending I know the answer?"

I smiled.

"Absolutely."

We used a pot with drainage holes and fresh soil. He loosened the old roots carefully, following my instructions with more patience than he'd shown his tea kettle the day before. I held the stem steady while he settled the new soil around it.

When he finished, he looked expectantly at the leaves.

Nothing happened.

"Is it cured?" he asked.

"Plants aren't obliged to perform gratitude."

"Tragic."

Mina returned with a small ledger she kept for the garden. It listed which herbs the kitchen actually used, how much water the courtyard needed in summer, and which beds belonged to the neighbor.

"The basil isn't a guest who can survive on compliments," she said.

Iroh looked stricken. "I have been most encouraging."

"Try a watering schedule."

We made one, with room to record whether the soil was still damp from the day before. Lian looked over the wall to say the watering can was dripping onto her bricks. Iroh lifted it, examined the loose spout, and asked whether she wanted him to fix it before making another puddle.

"Yes," she said. "And no more mystery vines."

I laughed. The vine labeled NOT TEA had become a minor legend, but it was also a reminder that we couldn't use plants simply because they smelled interesting. We called for a gardener to identify anything new before it went into a cup.

Iroh sat on the low stone bench when the work was done. He looked tired, but it wasn't a sad tiredness.

"I was once praised for taking cities," he said. "Today I have learned to water one small pot."

"Which are you more proud of?"

He looked at the curled leaves. "I think I know which one I want to remember."

I took his hand. I wanted to tell him he had become good, that everything harmful in his past had been repaired by growing basil. That would have been untrue. The work he'd done here mattered without paying for absolution from people he'd never met.

"May I sit with you?" I asked.

"You already are."

"Then may I stay after supper?"

His smile was almost shy. "If you wish."

"I do."

The shop would reopen tomorrow. The basil would need checking. We had other people, tasks and affections in our lives, and nothing about this little garden made those choices disappear. I leaned against his shoulder until the afternoon light moved off the wall.

We made a watering schedule on a scrap of paper. Mina had told us she couldn't leave the breakfast rush to inspect the pots, so we put the check after lunch. Iroh asked whether I wanted to do it every morning.

"Some mornings," I said. "Not all of them. I have other places to be, and sometimes the Threadway schedule changes."

He nodded.

We had talked about my ethical non-monogamy and preference for polyamory; the garden wasn't a symbol of exclusivity or ownership. He could care for it when I was away. I could return to find it changed. If either of us needed help, we could ask.

"Then I will keep the record when you're gone," he said.

"And let me see it when I come back."

"Without marking your answers wrong?"

"Let's not make promises we can't keep."

He laughed.

Lian returned with a small jar of cuttings she no longer had room to grow. The roots were white and strong.

"Do you want these?" she asked. "I can't put them near my drain. They spread too quickly."

Iroh looked tempted.

"They would look splendid along the wall."

"They would look splendid everywhere," Lian said. "That's the problem."

We examined the jar together. I had been thinking only about making our patch of green look fuller. I hadn't considered what would happen to the neighboring beds after a season of unchecked growth.

"What if we keep one in a separate pot?" I asked.

Lian nodded. "That could work if you cut off the seed heads and check it every week."

Iroh considered the extra work.

"Perhaps we have enough to care for already."

He thanked her and declined the cuttings.

It surprised me how much I liked that choice. A garden wasn't made better simply by collecting every beautiful thing that crossed its boundary.

When Lian had gone, I wrote a little note beside the watering schedule: *Before adding a plant, ask who will care for it.*

Iroh read it.

"Before offering advice," he said, "perhaps one should also ask who will live with it."

"Are you talking about gardening?"

"At this moment, yes."

He looked far too pleased with himself.

At dusk we sat beneath the climbing vine with two cups of tea. Iroh kept glancing at the basil.

"It still looks terrible," he said.

"Yes."

"Then I suppose we have done what we can."

"For today."

He held out his hand.

"Would you like company?"

"I would."

I moved close enough that our shoulders touched. He smelled of tea and fresh soil, and I caught a little dirt on his sleeve.

"May I kiss you?" I asked.

"Even in my present disreputable condition?"

"Especially then."

The kiss was warm, unhurried and a little awkward because his tea cup was still between us. We laughed, set it aside, and kissed again.

Later we went upstairs and closed the door. The garden needed nothing more from us that night.

Three mornings later, the basil sent out one new green leaf. Iroh came to find me before breakfast, delight bright in his eyes.

"Victory!" he announced.

I raised an eyebrow.

He looked toward the plant, then back at me.

"A promising development," he amended.

I kissed his cheek.

We made tea and allowed the garden to grow at its own pace.
